projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charles K. Rockow was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Charles K. Rockow. Mr. Rockow served in the U.S. Army with the 701st Tank Destroyer's Battalion. Charles served in North Africa and Italy, and his highest rank was Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Rockow's home in Madison, Ohio on October 4th 2002. Charles was 82 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: In Willoughby.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. And do you remember --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Vine Street. 359.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember December 7th 1941?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. I was in -- already in service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, you were already in.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you join?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were drafted in the pre-war draft.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then when were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Earlier in 1941.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Drafted into the Army.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Into Ft. Knox, Kentucky. Then I went from the new barracks to training barracks to the old 69th barracks. And that's when the war broke out. That's -- December 7th.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were at Ft. Knox on December 7th?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing that news?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, it just -- The war broke out. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't have any particular feeling about what was going on? You were expecting it?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah. But -- young guys, you know, Well, we're going over there and tear them people apart. But we never went over that direction.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: So we went from -- Ft. Knox, Kentucky, we went to Northern Ireland, and we stayed there for seven months, training. Then we went from there to England, stayed there two months. Then we went to Africa --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: -- to Oran. And had quite a battle at Oran, if you know anything about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me whatever you can about that. I know a little bit. I've heard some stories.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, they caught them out there with their pants down, you might say.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And they just killed a lot of men there, killed a lot of us. And then we got into Oran. And at that time, we had half tracks with 75s on them. And we battled up in there and got into Kasserine Pass, and that's when the Germans broke through our ____, and they run us back. We lost all our equipment, and we went in the desert, and we got re-equipped there with the N10s, and then we went on up through to Italy -- or, I mean, to Africa. And then from Africa, we went across to Italy. When we first went into Italy, why, the Italians, of course, was against us then. They'd spit at us or everything, you know. And then after a while when they found out they was -- we were with them and going ahead, you know, they'd throw flowers at the tanks and all kinds of stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your outfit?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: 701st tank destroyers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, was that your choice, or were you assigned to that?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: I was assigned to that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And what was your particular job?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, I went up to, as you saw here, I was sergeant of the tank.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were the commander of the tank?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Commander of the tank, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How big was the crew?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: We had five guys, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just so we get the dates, let's see. You probably landed in Africa in, what, late '42, October '42, somewhere around there?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Around there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fall, yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And then after we got straightened out, why, you know, we went through the chasing the Germans all the way through. Of course, it was -- it was Italians there, too?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In Africa.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We had -- What the heck was that guy's name? I can't think --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You're not thinking of Mussolini.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Mussolini.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Mussolini, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And we went through with the Desert Fox, you know. And when we got up to -- Oh, it was the other part of Italy, why, they caught up with him and found him, him and his girlfriend, there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, did you -- You landed directly in Italy. You didn't go to Sicily first, or did you?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: I didn't go to Sicily, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. All right.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No. I went to Naples.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what else can you tell me about the Italian campaign?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: About what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me -- stories about the Italian campaign?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, it was kind of rough. We was up in the mountains and down in the flatlands and all over the place. We went through -- with another tank outfit, and we was going up a mountain. It was a tank and a tank destroyer and another tank, and then I was behind that tank. But that first tank going up there hit the mine fields and just blowed it all up, blowed the whole tank up, killed the guys in there, and they were -- and we went through -- had a lot of different experiences, you know, going through there. And like I told you, I hit a -- hit a land mine, blowed the track off, and then we got -- I got another tank and then went on from there. We got a lot of close calls, you know. We slept in the ground a lot, dig a hole in the ground, put trees over the top, put the dirt over the top of that and put -- like that, you know, and then this way, because they'd come with them incendiary bombs, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And they dumped them down there, and if you didn't -- If you didn't make that an angle like that, then you'd -- you'd get hit with that shrapnel stuff. They'd drop down in the -- so you had to make that like that. And they'd come over at night -- (flange), you know, and they'd drop the bombs -- There was a place in Africa there they bombed us. They didn't hit nothing. We was out in the open range, and they come over and bombed us, high bombed. And they missed, oh, by, say, oh, from here to that building right there was one of the half tracks and about that far away, and the bomb made a big hole in the ground. And the captain come over to me and looked at it, and he says, Is that a -- What was it he said? That was -- No cigar -- But no cigar.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Close but no cigar.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other close calls you remember?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, yeah. There's a lot of close calls.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: The Germans fought over them 88s. You know, they'd hear that shrapnel line when it'd hit close, you know. And I don't know if you ever heard or not the guys made up that thing, The 88s are breaking up that old gang of mine? (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No. Somebody made a song like that?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: You know, when the guys are not doing anything, why, they'd sit around and -- singing songs and all kinds of stuff, you know. And if -- if you look in that book right there, there's a picture in there. I don't know if you can even find it offhand, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Guys sitting around?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: The guys -- These two guys together all the time, you know. And he's -- He's zipping up his jacket, you know, and it sounds like the shrapnel flying. (Laughter).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you don't remember any of those songs? You can't sing any, huh?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No. That's -- that's -- Them different people from different parts there -- You know, like hillbillies. They -- they sing different songs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. What other kinds of things did you do for entertainment during the breaks?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Just write letters.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get any shows where you were, USO shows, or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Shows?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: What kind of shows?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't know. USO shows?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, hell, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Small shows?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: We never --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They weren't going to come where you were, huh?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No. We were on the front line all the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No. They don't bring nothing up there. I saw Eisenhower up there one time. But he wasn't up in the front, but he was back in the rear, and he was kind of -- They had a bunch of guys down in a -- kind of a valley there. And had some guys shooting over the top of them, you know, training, Tell them guys to keep their head down, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: But that's the only time I ever saw him. But we had Bradley, and at first we had 'ol blood and guts Patton.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: That's when we lost everything we had at first, and, let's see. We had -- Then we had Bradley, and then we had -- They changed them. They had two or three other guys. And then Eisenhower, and I think -- I think we finished out with Eisenhower.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As the commander and chief, yes, but the supreme commander, right?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you saw Eisenhower where? In Italy or Africa? Where did you see Eisenhower?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: In Italy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was in Italy, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. In Italy I saw him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you never got close enough to talk to any of these guys or listen to any of these guys, right?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: You mean Eisenhower?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I mean, obviously, you, probably, couldn't talk to him, but you never --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: I was standing as close to me to you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, really? So you could listen to him. What did he say? Anything?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, he just still -- Keep your head down.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: You know, shooting over the top of you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: You know, you'd like to say, Well, why in the hell ain't you out there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of close buddies that you had?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. I had some buddies that got killed. Some buddies got their leg blowed off because, you know what a castrator is?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I've heard of that. Describe it. You can go ahead and describe it.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: It's a little thing like a fountain pen they put in the ground, you know, and put a trip on it, and when you walk over it, it blows your balls off. And guys hit the mine or walk on the mine, why, they get their leg blowed off or more, you know. And, let's see. Oh, the German land mine, 11 and three quarter pounds of TNT in that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: One time I had to take a mine detector -- You know what a mine detector is -- and go up the road looking for the mines. And you just sweat. (Laughter) And when you find a mine, they, generally, take the pin out of the top of the mine. There's a little thing on the top here to -- You know, they pull the pin out, and they'll, generally, lay the pin down next to the mine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And if you were to put that pin back in --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: -- you talk about sweat, boy, that's a sweat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So is that how they would disarm the mine, is put that pin back in?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: You put the pin back in there, and it wouldn't blow.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No. Why would they leave the pin next to it, in case they wanted to disarm it?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No. No. They --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: They'd just pull the pin and leave it lay there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh. That's just what they did.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They just pulled it.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: I wouldn't say they do that all the time, but that's -- that's the way it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But that's how the -- the -- What did they call those guys that would defuse the mines, whatever the -- whatever the -- the combat engineers, whatever, that's what they would do, though, they'd have to carefully stick that in, into the hole or whatever, on that mine and --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, most of the time they'd just put a -- ribbons, like, around the place --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: -- and say, This is a mine field. Stay away.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. A lot safer that way if people --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- stay away if you knew where the mine field was, right?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. But, like I said, they would plant mines where individuals could walk and -- and blow their leg off or something, you know, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any members of your tank crew?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Lots of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. We got -- They set up re-posts, you know, and replaced the guys, and then you have to start all over. You have to teach the guys what you're doing. And it was quite a thing. And one -- one outfit, I don't know if it was the 636 tank destroyers or the 601. I don't remember which one it was. But they were in a position where they were doing some shelling, you know, for the loader. He loaded up -- They left the breach open. And then he put the shell in there so far, you know, and left it lay there. So when they got the other thing -- a call to fire, he picked up another shell, and he shoved it in there and hit the detonator on that shell that was sitting in there, killed a whole bunch of them in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did any members of your crew make it through the whole time with you of the -- How big was the crew, again? Five-man crew?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Five men, yeah. Well, you know, had different guys. There were replacements because when somebody got hurt or taken back to the rear for some reason or other, why, they'd take them -- a guy that knowed what he was doing and put him in the other tank, make him a corporal or --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So some of your guys were taken away to --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Sergeant or whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They were put on other crews, then.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Some of the guys. Okay.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Then you'd get the new guys, see. So you'd have to teach them what you were doing. So that's the way it goes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did anybody last the whole time with you staying on the crew with you?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No, not really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They all got moved around?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: They got moved around, yeah. Yeah. Because at first, when I first went into -- I was driver, see. I drove the tanks around. So after a while, why, they made me the leader of the tank. Of course, the sergeant went along with it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: So then when I got up to Austria, we was going to have a little trouble with Tito up there, but then they called me in the office and says, Hey, you're going home. I said, Good. (Laughter) I'm ready. So that's how I got some of these pictures that I showed you there. I asked the captain if I could move the tanks around and take a picture of it with the crew, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then when was that? When did they tell you you could go home?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: When I was up in Austria.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When? Do you remember, approximately, the date?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, let's see.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It doesn't have to be the exact date, but would that be in '45, 1945?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. 1945, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before the war ended, officially?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, yeah. It's before the war ended, officially, but then -- or right after the war ended, and we went up there, and they were still going to give us a little trouble up there at Tito.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh. Yugoslavia.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No, in Austria there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tito. Okay. Oh, I thought -- Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And, anyway, that's when I -- They told me I was going home. So I went back and took some pictures. And I think the next day or something, why, they took me to the airport and got on this plane and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you married when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So do you remember getting letters from your wife?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would she write?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, just about what she was doing. She worked at ____ and run around with anybody that would go with her. So when I come back, why, we got divorced.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Then I remarried, and I had two kids, and we lived a pretty good life all the time. And, of course, she died then. And so I got my daughter and my son left. My son just left here last weekend. He was here with his family, And -- from Illinois.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember getting packages from home?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would they send?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Send just whatever, cookies, stuff, you know, whatever they thought --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you finally got home when? Sometime in 1945, middle of --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: I think it was in July.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In July, okay.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: I think so, because I remember it was warm -- hot weather yet and -- Yeah. I think it tells you on there what --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: On the --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: On the discharge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Do you have any memories of your homecoming when you got home and saw your family?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Didn't have much of a homecoming.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes. It says July '45.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, a lot of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead. Let's hear them.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, you run over a mine with a tank when you're inside that tank, boy, you think you got hit or something, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And when I come -- Me and one fellow, we run -- come out of the tank and run around. And as we was running around, Germans was firing short arms -- small artillery, or not artillery, but small arms at us, you know. And then we got around to a bank and got behind a bank, and then we took off from there later, you know. But there was a lot of times -- We was going up and retrieve some tanks, and the Germans knew we was in this field, and they kept firing small arms in that field, you know. And you hear them bullets zinging around you. And so I told the guys I was with, I says, I ain't going up there to get them tanks. To hell with them tanks. Because you got to look out for yourself, you know. But you go up there and retrieve the tanks, you get up there and there might be a German tank there close and fire at you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, my first day in combat? No, that's pretty hard to remember that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't remember any particular feeling the first day you realized it was real?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, we got up into these cactus. We was in a big cactus patch. When they run us out of that cactus patch, just left the stuff there, you know, and run out of there, and you run them needles in your legs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Them needles stayed in your legs for two weeks before they festered and you have to dig them out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. It was -- But, otherwise, I never got injured all the time I was in there. And, like I said, there was a lot of fellows did get injured, some killed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other memories of the Kasserine Pass?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. We sat there for a long time in Kasserine Pass and firing over our head, Germans firing artillery, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was Patton in charge at that point at the Kasserine Pass?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And he was -- They were pretty much overrun by the Germans, right?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. It was like I told you. We lost half of the division.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: You know, a division, that's a lot of men.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: We run -- Back then there was a general, a one-star general, there, and he said, Who told you guys to get running back here? He says, You're supposed to be out on the front line, he says. There's the front line, go --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any idea of how many vehicles, how many tank destroyers you went through during the war, how many different --

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: How many I went through?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. I went through four of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Four of them.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Three. Three. I went -- I told you, I went -- come back from the front one night or one morning. I was up there with my crew with a bunch of infantrymen. I came back. That was in Italy. And we come back, and the roads was real narrow there. And we come up ____, and there was a big wall here. Well, we come up there. We hit this wall, and the doggone road give away, and we rolled down the hill.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And nobody -- nobody got hurt in that because there was so many guys in the tank that when the shells came out, see, we had the place like under here, we'd keep 20 shells over there and 20 shells over here. When some of them shells came out, they didn't -- there was so many guys packed in that tank, that they didn't have no place to go.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: But nobody got hurt when that tank went down. So I got another tank then. And, let's see. Like I told you, I had to get another tank when I hit that land mine. And what was the third one? Oh, we got hit -- We was up in Italy, and I was firing -- There was a mountain right in front of us here, and after this -- There was a house, like, about down, maybe, from here to the end of the road down here. And I was firing down there because I saw some action down there, people running around down there. And -- And so they got tired of that. And this was in the wintertime, now. So the Germans started to fire, and they fired colored smoke shells, and they fired three shells, one over here, one over here, and the third one hit the tank just smack right in the middle, and it concaved the front there and knocked out one motor. See, at that -- that particular tank that we have was diesel motors.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And it knocked out the one motor so we had to get another tank then. But that's it. There was so many times when you crap your pants.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I imagine. Any other scary things that you remember that we haven't talked about yet?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. One time we was up there, and we was firing, like, artillery, and Germans had got our range, and they fired right over the top of us. They was firing at our tank, and they fired over the top of us and went about from here to the street behind us. They made a hole in there you could bury a car in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. And then our colonel went back there, looked at it, and while he was back there, why, they fired, and he got hurt. So that was the end of him. So when them shells are firing at you, you're scared all the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No, I don't think -- That about covers it, I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That covers it?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have one particularly close buddy that you hung around with?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: No. You hung around, generally, with all the guys that was in your tank.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In your crew, right.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah, in the crew, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you started getting replacements, did you -- were you still getting close to the guys, or did you not want to get too close to the guys?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, some of them you get close to and other ones -- You know, it's just like anything else. You don't like me, I don't care for you, so you go your way, and I go mine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So the situation didn't force you to become friends.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Yeah. But a lot of the time when we had nothing to do, why, we'd sit and play cards or something like that, you know, or, like I said, a lot of the guys, they'd sing. And some of them had instruments, you know, the mandolin and guitar and stuff that they played, and so -- It's something to while away the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'd love to hear one of those songs.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: You was eating C-Rations most of the time when you're up there. And I don't know if you know what C-Rations are.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why don't you describe that again, the C-Rations.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, in some of the cans it was like corned beef hash, and some of them -- What was in the other cans? One of the cans had -- they were like cookies in there, and then they had three or four pieces of hard candy there. Well, them cookies were so damned hard that you'd take and put it in the water and boil it and put the candies in the top there, you know, flavor it a little bit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: And so that's the way you ate them. And sometimes when you were close on the front line, why, you mingled with the Italians or -- The only thing that I ever got in Africa was oranges from some of them Arabs, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: But in Africa or in Italy, rather, you could get sausage and different stuff, you know, that you didn't know what the hell you were eating, but it was something better than what you had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: But when you get -- get away from the front line, why, then they set up a mess hall and you had a pretty good deal. So it wasn't any fun.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Are you proud that you went through it, though?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: Well, in a way. In a way. You go. Like, myself, I don't mix with them guys out there at the Legion or to the VFW because that's nothing but a ____ and a beer joint. That's all it is. That's all them guys go there for, to -- Of course, they have some meetings, and they go on parades and stuff like that. And I don't go for that. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. That's it?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: That's about it, I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Does that cover it?

sp.speaker: Charles K. Rockow
sp.p: That's about it, yeah.
